links.reason: 1050 is a doubtful verse about திகிரிப் புள்ளு parted at night; 1061 shows generic cock birds (புள்ளின் சேவலே) sheltering mates, with no separation theme. The contrast is plausible but the 'closing picture giving the night a second reading' is not in the Tamil.

Both use a simile of stars bereft of the moon: வெண்மதி யிழந்த மீன்போல் (1215) and மதியம் கெடுத்த வய மீன் (23), applied to the hero's friends and his brother. The shared figure shows both ends of the circle depend on him.

Kural 392 names two eyes, எண் and எழுத்து, not learning as 'the only eye of life'; the teaches misstates it. The epic's list is king, learning, sun and the verse leaves unclear which is set first, so the gains are vague.

Line 74 of Manimekalai reports ascetics who hold that a deed reaches its doer even without intention (சிந்தை இன்றியும் செய் வினை உறும்), while 1418 only says the fruit reaches its doer and no other. The pair concerns different axes (who receives vs. whether intention is needed), so the qualification is real but thin.
359 shows Vijayai waiting for news (வரும் வழி நோக்கி); 1785 shows her weeping while young men bow to her. That the news comes unrecognised 'from strangers' and the irony are not in either verse.

9 has the king deaf to counsel (சொல்லாறு கேளான்) and 27 the son who hears dharma (அறம் கேட்டு); these are different kinds of hearing and make no incompatible claim. Contrast of father and son, not tension.

Kural 365 says the free are those freed of craving (அவா அற்றார்); it does not say release comes at once, so 'the Kural joins' what the epic separates is not in the couplet. 409 (ஆர்வ வேரரிந்து ... நோற்றபின்) merely illustrates the order.
182 (the foe is killed) and 183 (பகை அறவே எறிந்து ... போர்வினை தவிர்கென) are plot sequence. The claim that the killing, not mercy, ends the war says nothing the order does not.

Both verses use iron turned to gold by fire (இரும்பின் ஈர்மை கெடுத்து எரி ... பொன்னாக்கிய / கொல்லுலை ... செம்பொனாகி). 960 reuses it to answer the doubt whether the dog can become a god, shifting the figure from gratitude to doctrine.

245 has a god giving a mantra to call on (மந்திரம் ... நினைக்க) and 16 has a god bidding Civakan think of him and teaching spells (நினைக்க என்று ... விஞ்சை). That is a recurring motif, not a distinctive image, and 16 does not show the later summoning.

Both open யாயாகியளே and have the friend say the wife hides the lord's கொடுமை out of shame. The poems are parallel, not one extending the other, and 10 has no wasting of the body, so the 'two costs' reading is built across two different poems.

28 names the brother, friends and wives who renounce, and 2640 shows renouncers learning the Anga books (அங்கநூல்) and shining as tilaka. The verse does not say who they are, but its place in the closing chapter supports the pairing.

829 has people wishing 'செய்தவம் நமக்கிசைக' (may his penance come to us), a wish to share the fruit; Kural 265 says tavam is practised because it yields what is wanted. 'The shortcut the couplet rules out' and a counter-case for the couplet are the grader's own extension.

1131 foretells a yaksha carrying Civakan off (கொண்டுபோம் இயக்கன்) and 1158 shows the lord lifting him away, a real fulfilment. But the teaches adds friends plotting by fire and disguise, which neither verse mentions.

1730 only reads pregnancy from a gem-dream; Tirumanthiram 453 says the Lord fixes the child's span at conception. Neither verse speaks to the other: nothing in the dream reads the child's fate, and a royal dream adds nothing to Tirumular's verse.

Kural 1157 has bangles slipping (இறவா நின்ற வளை) as a sign of his leaving; 1698 has bangles falling as he leaves (துறப்ப ... வளையும் தோடுறப்ப). The image is shared, but the 'three-stanza refrain' is not in the packet and the Kural gains nothing.

Neelakesi 131 (ஒழுக்கூற்றைப் பல்பண்டம் மூடினாய் தோலின்) and Manimekalai 67-68 (பூவினும் சாந்தினும் புலால் மறைத்து யாத்து) both unmask adornment as covering filth. The role reversal across the two epics is a fair observation.

528 (வரிசையா நோக்கின்) concerns a king's regard for kin by merit; 541 (கண்ணோடாது ... யார்மாட்டும்) concerns impartial judgment. These are different situations, not a tension, and the teaches (household vs. court) is not in either couplet.

1904 says the Jina cut the dark garlands of deeds (கருமாலை வெவ்வினைகள் நூறி), which echoes Kural 5's இருவினை, but the epic verse already states a result in line 4. The claim that each side gains what the other lacks is not specific.
334 has Vijayai hearing her son's future greatness from the deity; 1796 has Devadattan reciting his deeds. That Devadattan does not know she is the mother is not in the verse.

829 has the king decide (கொடுப்பனென்று) then consult kin (தமரோடு எண்ணி); Kural 676 is about weighing the finish, hindrance and yield, not counsel. A 'formality' reading is possible but the gains are stated as absences, not specific gains.

108 foretells a messenger with a letter coming into the garden, and 514 reads a letter, a real fulfilment. But the letter in 514 greets the lord of Podanam and sends gifts; it does not offer a bride, so the teaches is unsupported.

Both verses have the hero win the princess's vina contest (வீணையின் வென்று / யாழ்ப் படை பொரு), but 628 only has her going out to the contest. Two instances do not show a 'standard marriage test'; shared theme.

Kural 67 makes a father's good putting the son first in the assembly; 1743 hands a five-year-old to teachers (பொய்யாக் கல்விச் செல்வர்). It illustrates the couplet, and the epic verse does not state the purpose the gains give it.

1982 refuses the name மக்கள் to those without discernment; 1984 says the eunuch and blind are not counted, and that birth as a woman is not பீடுடைத்து (not honoured), which is not the same as 'not fully human'. The note misdescribes line 4.

Kural 336 says the world has the greatness of one gone today; Purananuru 356 shows the burning ground that has seen everyone's back. They agree on impermanence, but the claim that the ground is the couplet's 'greatness' equates two things the texts do not equate.

1747 recounts the promise to bring Nandattan to his lord's feet (அடிகள் பாதம் புல்ல யான் புணர்ப்பல் என்று ... விஞ்சை ஓதி ... இடுவித்திட்டாள்), and 1725 shows him lying at Civakan's feet. The later verse explains the earlier scene.

447 has the priest's instruction to make the slab and receive him (எழுந்தெதிர்கொள் என்ன நீங்கலன் இருந்தனன்) and 441 has the keeper offering it as 'நினக்கென வியற்றிய' seat. The keeper acts on the foretelling.
1204 puts the demand (இரண்டிலொன்று உரைமின்) and 1205 shows rage on hearing of the maid. This is immediate sequence, and 'cannot be accepted' is not stated; the teaches only restates the order.

664 has Kattiyankaran say only Kama could beat her at the vina; 674 has the narrator call Civakan அனங்கன் அன்னான் while adorning a dancer. A stock epithet in a different scene is not a refutation, so there is no tension or irony in the Tamil.

Soolamani 1380 despises the man who flees (அருவருப்புடைய ஆண்மை) and Purananuru 278 has the mother vowing to cut her breast for her son's reported flight. They share a warrior ethic, but the 'family shame' the epic is said to gain is not in 1380.

2667 is a toilette (நாவி நாறும் கூந்தலை உலர்த்தி ... மாலை) and Naladiyar 16 a lamb nibbling the garland before slaughter. Only the word 'garland' is shared; the epic garland is not bait, so the darker reading is imposed.

367 describes ponds thick with paste (அரிசனம் ... குங்குமக் குழம்பு) and Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal and garlands without knowing the body (படுசாந்தும் கோதையும்). The juxtaposition is real, but 367 does not praise the paste and the epic is not shown as 'delight'.

2326 has Civakan bathed as in blood and joined to the Earth; 2522 has him treading the kings' crowns (மன்னர் முடிமிதித்து ஏறினான்). 2326 is not a promise, so 'fulfilment' overstates; both show his sovereignty.

Kannaki's dream in 9:45-54 is told to Devanthi (not to Kovalan, as the note says), and the unit shows her unease, not that fate cannot be turned. A dream is the only shared element; the contrast of valence is stock.

316 has the deity telling the queen that one will come to take the child and that it is right to hide (கொண்டு போம் ஒருவன் இன்னே ... யாம் மறைவது கருமம்); 322 has Kantukkatan hurrying to the child. The prophecy and the command explain the mother's absence.

304 resolves on a vow (புண்ணிய நோன்பு நோற்க) and 309 has women showing desire as it begins (காமத்தை உருவு காட்டினார்). That the renunciation 'costs the king something' is not stated; the order is plot sequence.

Kural 1094 has her look at the ground when he looks; 1626 has her gaze fall on her own breasts when he looks at her face (முலை முகத்தை நோக்கும்). The gesture is shared, but 1626 does not call it a sign of love, and the Kural gains no memory-of-separation case.

Kural 333 says wealth does not stay and bids one do what does; 2983 says Fortune does not leave the unattached (திருமகள் என்று நீங்காள்) and will not come to one who clings (பற்றொடே நிற்பின் ... செல்லாள்). The epic adds a condition on the Kural's statement that wealth does not stay.
107 foretells a Vidyadhara king giving his daughter to the young lord, and 972 has the king say he has come gladly to give her (தருதற்கு மகிழ்ந்து வந்தேன்). The fulfilment adds willing consent.

393 has the teacher's fee that Civakan bear no anger for a year (அழற்சி இன்மை வேண்டுவல்), and 1090 has him bound, anger quenched, recalling it (உவாத்தி சொல்லால் ... சினந்தணிந்து). The later act is the keeping of the earlier promise.
1962 names flesh-sellers, crushers and hunters, and Neelakesi 104 names rain, battle, the chase for food and nets. The lists overlap only in part, and two examples do not show a stock teaching form.

1297 has Gunasenan roaming like a rutting elephant and 1304 opens on his fall (குணசேனன் வீழக் கண்டு). It is a reversal in time, not an incompatible claim, so tension is the wrong type; the 'boast' as test is not in the Tamil.
